# The Weight of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking lately about how we move through time without really noticing it. The way a Tuesday becomes a Friday, and suddenly you can't remember what you did on Wednesday. The way people age and you don't see it happening until someone says "Remember when we were in college?" and you realize that was somehow fifteen years ago.

There's something unsettling about this, but also something strangely beautiful.

I was sitting in a coffee shop this morning—one of those places with exposed brick and plants in the windows—and I watched a woman in the corner working on her laptop. She'd take a sip of coffee, type frantically for three minutes, then stare out the window for a while. Repeat. I wondered what she was writing. A novel? An email she was too nervous to send? A grocery list? The ordinariness of it struck me. She was just existing, just moving through her day the way we all do, and yet her life was as complex and full of stakes as anyone's.

I think we underestimate the weight of ordinary moments.

We're all waiting for something—for the big job, the right relationship, the moment when everything clicks into place and we finally feel like we've arrived. But what if we're already there? What if every moment is the moment, and we're just too distracted to notice?

I read somewhere that you can't step in the same river twice because the water is always flowing. You can't step in the same moment twice either, but we try. We replay conversations in our heads. We imagine different outcomes. We hold onto things, trying to preserve them in amber, not realizing that the preservation itself destroys what made them precious—which was their fleeting nature. Their impermanence. The fact that they mattered because they couldn't last.

My grandmother used to say that time moves faster the older you get because each year becomes a smaller fraction of your life. When you're five, a year is twenty percent of your existence. When you're fifty, it's two percent. Mathematically, it makes sense. But I think there's something else happening too. We stop paying attention. We stop noticing things because we've decided we already know what things look like, how they work, what they mean.

The first time you see the ocean, you stand there for hours probably. The hundredth time, you maybe glance at it while checking your phone.

I'm trying to be more present. I don't know if I'm doing a good job. I catch myself lost in thought about something that happened last week or something that might happen next month, and I have to consciously bring myself back to the here and now. It's harder than it sounds. Presence requires a kind of vulnerability—you have to actually feel what's happening rather than just moving through it on autopilot.

When you're really present, you notice strange details. Like the way the light falls at a specific angle in late afternoon. Like the particular sound of someone's laugh. Like how a song you've heard a thousand times suddenly hits different because you're actually listening to it instead of just letting it play in the background of your life.

I wonder if this is what people mean when they talk about living deliberately. Not making grand gestures or completely upending your life, but just paying attention. Just noticing the coffee shop, the light, the person next to you on the bus who looks like they're thinking about something complicated.

Everyone's thinking about something complicated. Everyone's carrying around their own invisible weight—their worries, their hopes, their private embarrassments and secret joys. The person at the grocery store checkout. The stranger walking past your window. The woman in the coffee shop with the laptop.

This is what we're all doing: showing up every day and trying to figure it out. Trying to be good, or at least good enough. Trying to make sense of things. Trying not to hurt people. Trying to matter. Sometimes succeeding, sometimes failing spectacularly.

I think that's worth noticing. I think that's worth taking seriously.

There's a line I love from a Mary Oliver poem: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" The question assumes that you have a plan, that you know what you're doing with it. But maybe that's not the right frame. Maybe the question isn't what grand plan you have, but whether you're actually showing up for it. Whether you're present for the one wild and precious life you're already living.

This moment, right now, is as precious as any moment you've ever had or will have. It's not a rehearsal. It's not a preparation for something else. It's not filler between the good parts. This is it. This is the good part.

I'm trying to remember that more often. I'm trying to be kinder to the people around me because I know they're struggling with something, even if I can't see it. I'm trying to be kinder to myself for the same reason. I'm trying to notice things—the smell of someone's perfume, the way sunlight looks through wet leaves, the exact tone of a friend's voice when they're about to tell you something they've been keeping inside.

These small things. These ordinary moments that don't seem like much until you really look at them, and then they seem like everything.

I don't have a conclusion here. I don't have the answer to how to live or how to find meaning or how to stop time from moving so fast that you blink and suddenly ten years have passed and you can barely remember where you were when. I'm still figuring it out, same as everyone else.

But I know this: the woman in the coffee shop with her laptop is doing something that matters to her. The coffee tastes like something. The light is falling a certain way. And we're all here, moving through these moments together, mostly trying our best, mostly failing to notice how beautiful and temporary and heavy and light everything is all at once.

Maybe that's enough to know.
